contentBlocks.title: Speeding & Speeding Over 100 MPH
contentBlocks.body: Speeding violations are common, but driving in excess of 100 MPH carries a separate and serious consequence in Minnesota. A conviction for driving over 100 MPH requires a six-month driver's license revocation, or a longer minimum period if another applicable law requires it. Andrew reviews the alleged speed, the traffic stop, the speed-measuring evidence, and whether there is a basis to challenge the charge or negotiate an outcome that better protects the client's driving privileges.

contentBlocks.title: Should You Go to Court for a Minnesota Speeding Ticket?
contentBlocks.body: Andrew generally recommends taking a traffic citation seriously rather than treating it as an automatic fine. Going to court may create an opportunity to challenge the citation, review the evidence, or discuss a resolution with the prosecutor. The right strategy depends on the charge, the driving record, whether a license or job is at risk, and what evidence supports the ticket.

contentBlocks.title: Can Radar or Speed-Measuring Evidence Be Challenged?
contentBlocks.body: Minnesota law sets conditions for admitting radar and other speed-measuring evidence. The operator must be sufficiently trained, must be able to explain how the device was set up and used, the device must have been operated with minimal distortion or interference, and it must have been tested by an accurate and reliable method when it was set up. Test records kept by law enforcement are available to a defendant on demand. Andrew reviews those records, the officer's report, video, and the circumstances of the stop for issues that may be worth litigating.

contentBlocks.title: What You Say During a Traffic Stop Can Matter
contentBlocks.body: A driver can unintentionally make the state's case easier by admitting the violation during the stop or later in court. Statements such as acknowledging that you were speeding may become evidence. Andrew's advice is to stay polite, avoid volunteering explanations or admissions, and get legal guidance before deciding how to address a citation that could affect your license, record, insurance, or employment.

contentBlocks.title: Illegal Lane Change
contentBlocks.body: Improper or unsafe lane-change citations can still affect a Minnesota driving record and may have insurance or employment consequences even though Minnesota does not use a traditional driver's-license point system. Andrew reviews the officer's observations, roadway conditions, dash-camera footage, and other evidence to determine whether the citation can be challenged or reduced.

contentBlocks.title: Careless and Reckless Driving
contentBlocks.body: Careless or reckless driving charges are more serious than standard traffic offenses and may result in criminal consequences. We analyze police reports, witness statements, and dash cam footage to build a strong defense and protect your record.

contentBlocks.title: Failure to Signal & Failure to Yield
contentBlocks.body: Small mistakes can lead to costly penalties. Many of these tickets are defensible, and our team works to keep them off your driving record and prevent insurance increases.

contentBlocks.title: Leaving the Scene of an Accident (Hit and Run)

A simple failure to exchange information can still lead to criminal charges. We investigate the circumstances, challenge assumptions, and work aggressively to reduce the impact on your life.

contentBlocks.title: Mobile Device and Hands-Free Violations

faq.q: Is criminal vehicular homicide the same as murder?

faq.q: Do I automatically go to prison if I am charged?

faq.q: What does the state have to prove in a Minnesota criminal vehicular homicide case?
faq.a: The state must prove the death was caused by operation of a motor vehicle under one of the statutory criminal-vehicular-homicide theories, such as gross negligence, specified impaired-driving conduct, an alcohol concentration of .08 or more, leaving the scene, or certain known vehicle defects. faq.q: What is the maximum penalty for criminal vehicular homicide in Minnesota?

faq.q: Can I restore my gun rights in Minnesota after a felony conviction?
faq.a: Sometimes, but the answer depends on the conviction and the specific state and federal prohibition. Minnesota provides a judicial restoration process for a person prohibited under state law because of a crime-of-violence conviction or delinquency adjudication if the statutory requirements are met and the court finds good cause. faq.q: Can I own a gun after a domestic assault conviction in Minnesota?
faq.a: Domestic assault convictions often trigger both state and federal firearm prohibitions. In some situations, you may be able to seek restoration through the court or challenge how the conviction is classified. Because federal law can still apply even if a state court restores your rights, it’s critical to have a lawyer who understands both layers. We look at the exact statute you were convicted under and how it interacts with federal law before taking any steps.

faq.q: What if my gun rights were taken because of an order for protection (OFP) or DANCO?
faq.a: Orders for protection and domestic abuse no-contact orders (DANCOs) can temporarily restrict your ability to possess firearms. Violations can also lead to new criminal charges. Once the order ends or is modified, you may be able to address firearm restrictions or seek restoration, depending on your full history. We help you understand how the order affects you now and what you can do going forward.

faq.q: What is the difference between state gun rights and federal gun rights?
faq.a: Minnesota law and federal law do not always line up. You could be eligible to restore your firearm rights under Minnesota law, but still be barred from possessing a firearm under federal law and the NICS background check system. A smart strategy considers both systems together so you don’t unintentionally commit a new crime by possessing a gun when federal law still says you cannot.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer for a weapons charge like carrying without a permit?

Even a first offense for carrying a handgun without a permit can be a gross misdemeanor, and repeat offenses can become felonies. An experienced defense lawyer can challenge the stop, the search, and whether the state can prove every element of the charge.

faq.q: How long does gun rights restoration take?

Most restoration petitions take several months because they involve gathering records, preparing a detailed petition, notifying agencies, and appearing in court. The more complex your history, the more preparation is required. We walk you through each step and give you a realistic sense of the process.

faq.q: Does expungement automatically restore gun rights in Minnesota?

faq.q: What exactly is a DANCO in Minnesota?
faq.a: A Domestic Abuse No-Contact Order (DANCO) is a court order prohibiting any contact   direct or indirect   with the alleged victim in a domestic-related case. This includes texts, calls, social media, being physically near them, or communication through third parties. Only a judge can modify or remove a DANCO, even if the alleged victim wants contact.

faq.q: Can I be charged if the alleged victim contacted me first?
faq.a: Yes. The protected person contacting first does not automatically make responding lawful. A DANCO remains in effect until the court changes or removes it. If the protected person reaches out, the safest course is to stop communication, preserve the messages, and speak with an attorney before responding further.

faq.q: Is a DANCO violation a felony?
faq.a: It depends on your history. A first-time violation is a misdemeanor (up to 90 days in jail and a $1,000 fine). One prior within 10 years makes the new charge a gross misdemeanor (up to one year in jail and a $3,000 fine). Two or more priors within 10 years make it a felony (up to 5 years in prison and a $10,000 fine).

faq.q: How can the state prove a DANCO violation?
faq.a: These cases are often proven through recorded jail calls, text messages, screenshots, phone logs, social media communication, witness reports, or police observation. Because the evidence is often digital, prosecutors move fast   and mistakes are common. We review every detail for weaknesses and unlawful police actions.

faq.q: Can a DANCO be modified or removed?
faq.a: Yes, but only by a judge. Your attorney can file a motion to modify the order, which may allow contact, limited contact, or contact regarding children. The alleged victim cannot remove the order themselves.

faq.q: What should I do if I accidentally violated the order?
faq.a: Stop all communication and call an attorney immediately. Do not send follow-up messages, explanations, or apologies   these will be used against you. Fast legal action can often prevent additional consequences, negotiate your release, or begin modifying the order.

faq.q: What is the difference between a DANCO and an Order for Protection in Minnesota?
faq.a: A DANCO is a criminal court order that can restrict contact while a criminal case is pending. An Order for Protection (OFP) is a separate civil order. The restrictions and procedures are different, so it is important to read the actual order and understand which type applies to your situation.

faq.q: Can third-party contact count as a DANCO violation?
faq.a: Yes. A DANCO can prohibit indirect contact, including asking another person to deliver a message to the protected person. Whether a violation can be proven depends on the facts, including what was said, who delivered the message, and what evidence shows where the communication originated.

contentBlocks.body: A DANCO can prohibit indirect contact as well as direct contact. Asking a friend, family member, or another person to deliver a message to the protected person can create a violation allegation. Andrew looks closely at what was actually said, who delivered the message, text or social media evidence, and whether the state can show that the communication originated with the person subject to the DANCO.
Even if the alleged victim asks to reconcile, wants to talk, or wants the order removed, the order remains fully active until the court says otherwise.

contentBlocks.title: Penalties for DANCO Violations in Minnesota
contentBlocks.body: Penalties increase dramatically based on your record:

items.text: Up to 90 days in jail and a $1,000 fine.
Up to 1 year in jail and a $3,000 fine.

items.lead: Felony (two or more priors within 10 years)
items.text: Up to 5 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

contentBlocks.body: Each contact can be charged separately, meaning multiple texts can result in multiple charges.

contentBlocks.title: Why These Cases Are So Easy to Violate
contentBlocks.body: DANCO violations often arise from situations people do not realize can create a problem. The protected person contacting first does not automatically make a response lawful, and indirect messages through other people can also lead to allegations. Common situations include:
items: The alleged victim reaches out first
Parents share children and need to coordinate schedules
A mutual friend passes along a message
Accidental run-ins happen in small communities
Emotions run high during breakups or pending domestic assault cases
Phone numbers are not blocked correctly

contentBlocks.title: How We Defend DANCO & OFP Violations
contentBlocks.body: Andrew looks at the facts surrounding the alleged contact and what the state can actually prove. That may include:
items: Whether the contact was direct, indirect, accidental, or unavoidable
Whether the protected person initiated the contact
Whether a third party actually delivered a message and where that message originated
Text messages, screenshots, social media activity, phone logs, or other digital evidence
Whether police or prosecutors misinterpreted the communication
Whether law enforcement had probable cause for the arrest
Whether a motion to modify the order is appropriate
How the alleged violation relates to the underlying domestic or criminal case

contentBlocks.body: Our goal is to reduce or dismiss the charge, protect your criminal record, and stabilize your situation so you can move forward safely.

contentBlocks.title: If You Have a DANCO or OFP, Do This Immediately

steps.step: Stop communicating with the protected person, even if they contact you first.
Save texts, messages, social media records, voicemails, and other evidence related to the contact.
Do not send follow-up explanations, apologies, or messages trying to fix the situation.
Exercise your right to remain silent and avoid discussing the allegation with law enforcement before speaking with a lawyer.
Contact a criminal defense attorney who can review the order, the alleged communication, and whether the order should be modified.

faq.q: What makes a domestic assault a felony in Minnesota?

faq.q: What is the maximum penalty for a gross-misdemeanor domestic assault in Minnesota?

contentBlocks.title: What Counts as Domestic Assault in Minnesota?
contentBlocks.body: Minnesota domestic assault uses the same two core assault theories seen elsewhere in state law, but the alleged victim must be a family or household member as defined by statute. The state may allege either an intentional act causing fear of immediate bodily harm or death, or an intentional infliction or attempted infliction of bodily harm. A visible injury is therefore not required in every prosecution.

contentBlocks.title: Who Is Considered a Family or Household Member?
contentBlocks.body: The domestic-assault statute incorporates Minnesota's family-or-household-member definition. Depending on the relationship, it can include:
items: Current or former spouses
Parents and children
People related by blood
People who are currently living together or have lived together in the past
People who have a child together or share a pregnancy, regardless of marriage or cohabitation
People involved in a qualifying significant romantic or sexual relationship

contentBlocks.title: Penalties for Domestic Assault
contentBlocks.body: Domestic assault is an enhanceable offense, meaning qualified prior domestic-violence-related convictions or delinquency adjudications can increase the level of the new charge.
items: Misdemeanor: a standard domestic-assault conviction can carry up to 90 days in jail and a $1,000 fine.
Gross Misdemeanor: a new domestic assault within ten years of a previous qualified domestic-violence-related offense can carry up to 364 days in jail and a $3,000 fine.
Felony: a new domestic assault within ten years of the first of two or more previous qualified domestic-violence-related offenses can carry up to 5 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

contentBlocks.title: DANCO and No-Contact Orders Can Affect Daily Life Immediately
contentBlocks.body: A domestic-assault case can involve a Domestic Abuse No Contact Order or other release conditions before the criminal charge is resolved. The exact order controls. Restrictions may affect returning home, direct communication, social media, or messages sent through another person. Even when the protected person wants contact, the defendant should follow the court order until a judge changes it.

contentBlocks.title: Can the Alleged Victim Drop a Domestic Assault Charge?
contentBlocks.body: The alleged victim can communicate their wishes and provide information, but the criminal case belongs to the state. The prosecutor decides whether charges continue. A request to dismiss can matter to the prosecutor's evaluation, but it does not automatically end the case or cancel a DANCO or release condition.

contentBlocks.title: Evidence Andrew Reviews in Domestic Assault Cases

contentBlocks.title: What to Do If You’re Charged With Domestic Assault

Save messages, call logs, photos, or evidence that may counter the accusations.

contentBlocks.title: What Happens After a Domestic 911 Call?
contentBlocks.body: A 911 call often becomes one of the first pieces of evidence in a domestic-assault case. Officers may separate the parties, obtain statements, photograph injuries, review the scene, and make an arrest decision based on probable cause and Minnesota's domestic-abuse arrest rules. Andrew reviews the recording and body-camera footage rather than relying only on the written police report, because differences in timing, wording, demeanor, injuries, and witness accounts can become important later.

faq.q: Are white collar crimes really treated as seriously as violent crimes?
faq.a: Yes. Even though they are non-violent, white collar offenses often carry long prison sentences, six-figure fines, restitution orders, and permanent damage to your career and reputation.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer if I’ve only received a subpoena or target letter?
faq.a: Absolutely. If you’re being asked for records or called in for an interview, you’re already on the radar. A lawyer can deal with investigators for you, protect your rights, and sometimes resolve matters before charges are filed.

faq.q: Can I talk to my employer or coworkers about the investigation?
faq.a: You should not discuss details of the investigation with anyone until you’ve spoken with a lawyer. Well-intended conversations can create misunderstandings, new witnesses, or allegations of obstruction.

faq.q: Are white collar cases always federal?
faq.a: No. Many financial crimes are charged in Minnesota state court. Others are brought federally, and some involve both. Your defense strategy will depend on where the case is filed and which agencies are involved.

faq.q: Should I talk to investigators before I hire a lawyer?
faq.a: It is almost always better to speak with a lawyer before you talk with law enforcement, auditors, or investigators about suspected fraud or financial misconduct. Even statements you believe are harmless can be misunderstood or taken out of context. Andrew can help you decide whether to give a statement, how to do so safely, or whether it is better to decline an interview altogether.

faq.q: What is the difference between a subpoena, search warrant, and target letter?
faq.a: A subpoena generally requires testimony or production of specified records. A search warrant authorizes law enforcement to search for items within the warrant's scope. A federal target letter can notify a person that prosecutors consider them a target of a grand-jury investigation. Each calls for a different response, and it is useful to have counsel review the document before acting.

faq.q: Can a bookkeeping mistake become a criminal fraud case?
faq.a: A mistake by itself is not the same as criminal intent. The government must prove the elements of the specific offense charged, which can include knowledge or intent requirements. Accounting records, authorization, communications, business practices, and who controlled the money can be important in distinguishing a mistake or dispute from criminal conduct.

contentBlocks.title: What Is a White Collar Crime?
contentBlocks.body: White collar crimes are non-violent offenses that typically involve money, property, or confidential information. They often arise out of business, employment, government, or financial relationships and may be investigated by local law enforcement, state agencies, or federal authorities. Even a single allegation of dishonesty can threaten your career, professional license, and standing in the community.

contentBlocks.title: State or Federal? White Collar Cases Can Go Either Way

The investigating agency, subpoena or warrant, alleged conduct, movement of money or communications, and statutes identified in the investigation can help show which system is involved.

contentBlocks.title: What Evidence Drives a White Collar Case?
contentBlocks.body: These cases often turn on records and context rather than a single eyewitness. Andrew may need to organize and compare:
items: Bank statements, transaction histories, checks, invoices, and payment records
Accounting systems, ledgers, expense reports, and audit materials
Emails, text messages, internal chats, and other communications
Contracts, policies, authorization records, and job responsibilities
Computer access logs, account credentials, metadata, and device records

Statements from coworkers, business partners, clients, auditors, or investigators
The flow of money and whether the records actually establish personal knowledge, intent, or benefit

contentBlocks.title: Intent Can Be the Central Dispute
contentBlocks.body: Many fraud, theft, embezzlement, and false-statement offenses require the government to prove a particular form of knowledge or intent. A suspicious transaction or accounting problem is not automatically proof of criminal intent. Andrew looks at authorization, business practices, who controlled accounts, what the client knew at the time, communications, accounting treatment, and whether there is a noncriminal explanation for the records.

contentBlocks.title: What to Do If You’re Under Investigation or Charged
contentBlocks.body: Early decisions in a white collar case can make the difference between a negotiated resolution and a conviction. If you think you’re being investigated or have already been charged:

steps.step: Do not talk to investigators, agents, or auditors without a lawyer present   politely invoke your right to counsel.
Contact an experienced white collar defense attorney immediately, even if you have only received a subpoena, letter, or phone call from an investigator.
Preserve all potential evidence, including emails, messages, financial records, and electronic files   do not delete or alter anything.
Avoid discussing the case with coworkers, clients, or friends; those conversations can be subpoenaed or used against you.
Work closely with your attorney to review the paper trail, understand your exposure, and develop a strategy tailored to your role and your goals.

contentBlocks.title: Investigations Versus Formal Charges
contentBlocks.body: A white collar matter may begin with an internal investigation, audit request, subpoena, search warrant, target letter, or contact from law enforcement. Those events mean different things. A subpoena generally demands testimony or records; a search warrant authorizes a search within its scope; and a target letter can indicate that federal prosecutors believe a person is a target of a grand-jury investigation. Andrew reviews the document or contact before the client responds and helps preserve records without making unnecessary statements.

contentBlocks.title: Do Not Delete or “Clean Up” Records After Learning of an Investigation
contentBlocks.body: Once an investigation, subpoena, audit, or litigation hold is known, deleting messages, altering files, backdating records, or asking others to change documents can create serious additional problems. Preserve potentially relevant material and let counsel determine what must be produced, what is protected, and how to respond lawfully.

faq.q: What makes a crime a federal case instead of a state case?
faq.a: A case may go federal when it involves federal statutes, federal land, crosses state lines, uses federal systems like the mail or wire transfers, or involves large-scale drug, fraud, or conspiracy allegations. Some conduct can be charged in either state or federal court or both depending on how the government chooses to proceed.

faq.q: Can I be prosecuted in both federal and state court for the same conduct?
faq.a: Yes. Under the “dual sovereignty” doctrine, state and federal governments are treated as separate sovereigns. That means the same conduct can lead to both state and federal prosecutions without violating the constitutional protection against double jeopardy. This is one reason you need a defense lawyer who understands both systems.

faq.q: Should I talk to federal agents if they want to interview me?
faq.a: You should not speak with federal agents or investigators without a lawyer present. Even honest, innocent answers can be misunderstood or used against you later. A federal criminal defense attorney can communicate with agents on your behalf, control the flow of information, and help protect you from accidental self-incrimination.

faq.q: Are federal sentences always harsher than state sentences?
faq.a: Federal sentences can be longer than state sentences for similar conduct, especially in drug, fraud, and gun cases. But the outcome depends heavily on the guideline calculations and how your lawyer presents your story. By challenging the government’s version of events and highlighting your personal history and mitigating factors, Andrew works to secure the lowest reasonable sentence – and in some cases, to avoid a conviction or prison altogether.

faq.q: Are the Federal Sentencing Guidelines mandatory?
faq.a: No. The Federal Sentencing Guidelines are advisory, but a federal judge must correctly calculate and consider the applicable guideline range along with the other sentencing factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a). Statutory mandatory minimums are separate and apply only when the charged and proven offense triggers one.

faq.q: What should I do if I receive a federal target letter or grand jury subpoena?
faq.a: Do not ignore it and do not assume you should immediately explain yourself to investigators. Preserve the letter or subpoena, note any deadline, avoid destroying or altering records, and have federal defense counsel review the document and contact the appropriate prosecutor or agent before you respond.

contentBlocks.title: Facing Federal Charges in Minnesota
contentBlocks.body: Federal cases use different procedures, agencies, charging documents, discovery practices, and sentencing rules than Minnesota state cases. Investigations may involve the FBI, DEA, IRS-CI, ATF, Homeland Security Investigations, inspectors general, or other federal agencies depending on the allegation. Early legal advice can be especially important before an agent interview, grand-jury subpoena, search-warrant response, surrender, detention hearing, or indictment.

contentBlocks.title: Target Letter, Grand Jury Subpoena, Search Warrant, or Agent Interview?
contentBlocks.body: The first sign of a federal case can take several forms, and each requires a different response:

items.text: An investigator may ask to speak voluntarily. Counsel can determine the client's status and communicate with agents before any interview occurs.
A subpoena may require documents or testimony and comes with deadlines and legal obligations that should be reviewed promptly.
A target letter can indicate that prosecutors believe substantial evidence links the recipient to a federal offense being investigated by the grand jury.
A warrant authorizes agents to search within its stated scope. The warrant, inventory, seized devices or records, and manner of execution should be preserved for review.
Once charges are filed, immediate issues can include initial appearance, detention or release, discovery, motion deadlines, plea discussions, and trial preparation.

contentBlocks.title: Common Types of Federal Crimes
contentBlocks.body: Many charges that could be handled in state court are instead brought in federal court because they involve interstate activity, federal programs, or large amounts of money or drugs. Davis Defense represents clients facing a wide range of federal allegations, including:
items: White collar and financial crimes: wire fraud, mail fraud, bank fraud, securities fraud, mortgage fraud, health care fraud, tax offenses, embezzlement, money laundering, public corruption, and related conspiracy charges.
Drug crimes: large-scale drug trafficking and distribution, conspiracy cases, alleged drug importation, and cases involving interstate or multi-defendant investigations.
Internet and technology offenses: computer crimes, online fraud schemes, identity theft, certain child-exploitation offenses, and cases involving interstate electronic communications.
Violent and organized crime: robbery of federally insured banks, weapons offenses with a federal component, RICO and gang-related prosecutions.
Cases on federal property or involving federal interests: conduct on federal land, in federal buildings, or involving federal employees or programs.

contentBlocks.title: Why Federal Cases Are So High-Stakes
contentBlocks.body: Federal offenses can carry significant statutory penalties, and some statutes include mandatory minimum sentences. In cases that reach sentencing, the court calculates an advisory range under the United States Sentencing Guidelines and then considers that range along with the other factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a). Because guideline calculations can be affected by offense-specific facts, criminal history, role, loss or drug quantity, acceptance of responsibility, and other provisions, disputes about the correct calculation can materially affect the sentencing analysis.

contentBlocks.title: How Davis Defense Handles Federal Cases
contentBlocks.body: Federal defense requires a clear picture of both the evidence and the procedural posture. Depending on the case, Andrew's work can include:
items: Determining whether the client is a witness, subject, target, or already charged defendant
Communicating with agents and prosecutors and evaluating interview requests
Reviewing subpoenas, warrants, discovery, financial records, digital evidence, and witness statements
Challenging unlawful searches, statements, or other evidence when supported by the facts and law
Analyzing the statute of conviction, mandatory-minimum exposure, and the applicable advisory guideline calculation
Negotiating when a resolution serves the client's goals while preparing the case for motions or trial when necessary
Presenting guideline objections and arguments under the federal sentencing factors when a case reaches sentencing

contentBlocks.title: What to Do If You’re Under Federal Investigation
contentBlocks.body: The choices you make early in a federal investigation can shape the entire outcome of your case. If you suspect or know that you’re being investigated:
steps: Do not talk to federal agents, investigators, or prosecutors without an attorney present even if they say they “just want to clear something up.”
Avoid discussing the situation by text, email, social media, or recorded jail calls; assume anything you say may be reviewed later.
Gather and preserve any documents, messages, or records that may help your defense, but do not destroy or alter anything the government might request.

contentBlocks.title: Charged in Federal Court? Davis Defense Can Help.
contentBlocks.body: If you have already been indicted or received notice of federal charges, time is critical. contentBlocks.title: How Federal Sentencing Works
contentBlocks.body: Federal sentencing begins with the statutes governing the conviction and a calculation of the advisory United States Sentencing Guidelines. The guideline calculation can depend on offense-specific factors and criminal history, while mandatory minimums apply only when a statute provides one. The judge must also consider the factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a) before imposing a sentence that is sufficient but not greater than necessary. Andrew reviews the guideline calculation, challenges unsupported enhancements or factual assumptions, and develops mitigation and variance arguments grounded in the client's history and the circumstances of the case.

faq.q: What is considered a juvenile case in Minnesota?
faq.a: In Minnesota, a juvenile case generally involves a person under 18 who is accused of conduct that would be a crime if committed by an adult. These cases are handled in juvenile court, which is a separate system focused on accountability and rehabilitation rather than pure punishment.

faq.q: Can my child be tried as an adult?
faq.a: Yes, in qualifying felony cases. Minnesota law permits adult certification proceedings for children age 14 or older, with different presumptions and burdens depending on age, offense, prior history, and other statutory factors. Some serious cases may instead proceed as Extended Jurisdiction Juvenile matters.

faq.q: Will a juvenile case be part of my child’s permanent record?
faq.a: Juvenile matters are treated differently from adult convictions and are often confidential, but that does not mean they have no impact. Certain felony-level juvenile findings can be visible, and a juvenile record can affect education, employment, housing, and even future background checks. In some cases, expungement or sealing may be possible, but it’s critical to protect your child’s record from the start.

faq.q: What is Extended Jurisdiction Juvenile (EJJ)?
faq.a: EJJ is a special prosecution path for specified felony cases involving a child who was 14 to 17 at the time of the alleged offense. An EJJ prosecution includes a right to a jury trial, and a conviction can result in a juvenile disposition plus a stayed adult criminal sentence that can be put at risk if the juvenile disposition is later revoked.

faq.q: Do we really need a lawyer if it’s ‘just’ juvenile court?
faq.a: Yes. Juvenile cases can involve detention, lengthy probation, out-of-home placement, loss of driving privileges, and long-term consequences for school and work. Having an experienced juvenile defense lawyer can influence everything from whether charges are filed, to the outcome at trial, to how serious the disposition is   and whether your child’s future opportunities remain open.

faq.q: Does my child have a right to a jury trial in juvenile court?
faq.a: Ordinary juvenile delinquency trials are generally tried to a judge rather than a jury. Extended Jurisdiction Juvenile prosecutions are different: Minnesota law provides a right to a jury trial in EJJ proceedings.

faq.q: What is the difference between EJJ and adult certification?
faq.a: EJJ keeps the case in a special juvenile-court track but can impose a juvenile disposition together with a stayed adult sentence. Adult certification moves a qualifying felony case into adult criminal court. The applicable standards depend on the child's age, the offense, and other statutory factors.

contentBlocks.title: Juvenile Charges Are Different — and So Is the Process
contentBlocks.body: Minnesota delinquency court has its own rules and terminology. A child may be alleged delinquent rather than charged and convicted in the same way as an adult, and the court has a broad range of dispositions focused in part on rehabilitation and public safety. Serious felony cases can follow additional paths, including Extended Jurisdiction Juvenile prosecution or adult certification. contentBlocks.title: How the Juvenile Court Process Works
contentBlocks.body: The path depends on the allegation, age, custody status, and whether the prosecutor seeks EJJ or adult certification. A typical delinquency case may involve:

items.text: The case may begin with a delinquency petition or citation alleging conduct that would be criminal if committed by an adult.
If the child is held, court rules require prompt judicial review of detention and release conditions.
The court advises the child of the allegations and rights, and the case can proceed based on an admission or denial.
Counsel can obtain discovery, litigate legal issues, challenge evidence, and discuss diversion or negotiated outcomes when available.
Ordinary delinquency trials are generally to the court, while an Extended Jurisdiction Juvenile prosecution carries a right to a jury trial.
If allegations are admitted or proved, the court chooses a juvenile disposition based on the offense, the child's circumstances, public safety, and available rehabilitative options.

contentBlocks.title: Possible Consequences in Juvenile Court
contentBlocks.body: Juvenile courts have a wide range of options, from light supervision to secure placement. Depending on the offense, history, and attitude of the child, the court can order:
items: Verbal warnings and informal supervision
Fines and restitution to victims
Community service and programming
Counseling, chemical dependency treatment, or mental health services
Probation with strict rules and monitoring
Out-of-home placement, foster care, or residential programs
Short-term or extended detention in a juvenile facility

contentBlocks.body: In serious cases, the court can also consider Extended Jurisdiction Juvenile (EJJ), which combines a juvenile disposition with a stayed adult sentence that can remain in place until approximately age 21.

contentBlocks.title: How a Juvenile Case Can Affect Your Child’s Future
contentBlocks.body: Juvenile records and dispositions are treated differently from adult convictions, but a case can still affect important parts of a young person's life. Depending on the allegation and outcome, issues can include:
items: School discipline, suspension, transfer, or extracurricular consequences
Probation, treatment, programming, or out-of-home placement
Driver's-license consequences in qualifying cases
Firearm consequences for certain adjudications
Public-record or background-check consequences in categories where juvenile records are accessible
Immigration consequences for noncitizens
Future EJJ, certification, sentencing, or criminal-history implications in later cases

contentBlocks.title: Extended Jurisdiction Juvenile (EJJ) & Adult Certification
contentBlocks.body: Minnesota law provides two important paths that can increase the stakes of a serious juvenile felony case:

items.text: EJJ applies in specified felony cases involving children who were 14 to 17 at the time of the alleged offense. An EJJ prosecution includes juvenile-court protections plus a right to a jury trial, and a conviction can result in both a juvenile disposition and a stayed adult criminal sentence. Violating the EJJ disposition can put the stayed adult sentence at risk.

For a child age 14 or older accused of a felony, the prosecutor may seek certification for adult prosecution when the statutory requirements are met. The rules include different presumptions and burdens depending on age, offense, prior history, and other factors. Whether the case remains juvenile, becomes EJJ, or is certified can be one of the most consequential decisions in the case.

contentBlocks.title: Can Police or School Officials Question My Child?
contentBlocks.body: A juvenile investigation may involve police, school-resource officers, administrators, or child-protection personnel. The child's age, custody status, who is asking questions, and the setting can affect the legal analysis. Families should avoid assuming that an informal-looking school or police conversation has no consequences. Andrew can review what has already been said and advise about future interviews before additional statements are made.

contentBlocks.title: What to Do If Your Child Has Been Charged
contentBlocks.body: Early organization can help protect both the case and the child's day-to-day life.
steps: Do not encourage your child to explain the allegation to police, school-resource officers, alleged victims, or witnesses before getting legal advice.
Save citations, petitions, release paperwork, school notices, messages, videos, social-media material, and other records related to the incident.
Write down the timeline and names of possible witnesses while events are fresh, without coaching anyone about what to say.
Follow release conditions, school restrictions, and court dates carefully while the case is pending.
Have counsel determine whether the case is ordinary delinquency, EJJ, or at risk of adult certification and build strategy around that path.
